title: Highlands Ranch Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: See Highlands Ranch well depths, yields, water levels and drilling costs, including a 205-foot median and finished-well estimates.
h1: What Highlands Ranch Wells Really Look Like
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Highlands Ranch means looking beyond the presence of a well permit. Records within five miles show a wide range of depths, water levels and well uses. The median reported depth is 205 feet, but the middle half runs from 40 to 526 feet. Some wells reach 2,668 feet.

This page uses Colorado DWR permit records for Highlands Ranch and nearby areas including Acres Green, Littleton, Louviers, Columbine Valley, Sterling Ranch and Lone Tree. The records are useful for setting expectations, but a neighboring well is not a guarantee for your lot. Local geology, the target aquifer, construction details and the driller's site evaluation still control the result.

sections.heading: Highlands Ranch well depth depends on the target formation
sections.html:
Reported well depth has a broad spread in the Highlands Ranch area. The median is 205 feet, while the middle half falls between 40 and 526 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 952 feet, and the deepest record reaches 2,668 feet.

The depth mix is unusual enough that a simple local average would not be a good bidding tool. Forty-five percent of wells are under 100 feet, while 24% fall from 300 to 600 feet and 21% are 600 feet or deeper. Only 10% are in the 100-to-300-foot range. The records identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers most often, followed by Denver and Arapahoe aquifers. A driller will need to evaluate the planned site and intended aquifer before giving a reliable depth allowance.

sections.heading: What a Highlands Ranch well may produce
sections.html:
Among the wells reporting pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Fifty-eight percent report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 40% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, while 2% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

That is a strong permit-record picture, but only 625 wells report a pump yield. Yield testing, storage and the proposed household demand still matter. A domestic well must also follow its permit conditions. An exempt household-use well has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, even if the formation could produce more.

sections.heading: Water levels in Highlands Ranch need careful reading
sections.html:
The reported static water level has a median of 198 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 40 to 405 feet. This is not the same as well depth: a well can be drilled below the water level to provide usable storage and reach a productive zone.

The decade series is uneven rather than a clear straight-line decline. The median measured level was 209 feet below surface in the 1980s, 720 feet in the 2010s and 190 feet in the 2020s. Because only 72 records report a static water level, and measurement conditions can differ, the 2010s result should not be treated by itself as proof that the water table is dropping. Ask for the actual static and pumping levels from nearby wells and compare dates, construction and aquifer.

sections.heading: Permit history and active drillers near Highlands Ranch
sections.html:
Permit records show construction activity across several generations. Permits issued totaled 76 in the 1950s, 46 in the 1960s, 276 in the 1970s, 358 in the 1980s, 697 in the 1990s, 783 in the 2000s, 265 in the 2010s and 116 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The records list 3,326 wells in total, with 1,495 recorded as constructed. Three drillers appear most often: Authorized (Pe, Pg), Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.) and Hier Drilling Co. (Hier, Peter J). Those names show permit-record activity, not a recommendation or proof that any one company is available for a new job. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scheduling and experience with the formation at your specific Highlands Ranch address.

sections.heading: What drilling a Highlands Ranch well may cost
sections.html:
The cost model uses Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the local median depth of 205 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at about $10,200 to $14,400. That is only the hole, not a complete operating water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at about $16,200 to $26,400 at the median depth. The broad local depth range means a bid based only on the median can miss badly if the site requires a deeper hole. Request a written estimate that separates drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, trenching, power and any difficult-access work. Verify what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than expected.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying in Highlands Ranch
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main signal in these records, but the data are incomplete: only 625 wells report pump yield, and a permit record does not replace a current flow test. Dry holes, poor construction or an unsuitable target zone can still occur. Fractured-bedrock wells are especially difficult to predict because water may depend on individual fractures.

Water quality also deserves direct testing. Mapped environmental records within about ten miles include 205 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 25 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 18 historic mine features. These mapped sites do not establish contamination at a particular parcel. Test the well for contaminants relevant to the location and review casing, grout, wellhead protection and septic separation with qualified professionals. Confirm that the proposed home, septic system and well can fit on the lot without creating a maintenance problem.

sections.heading: A practical Highlands Ranch lot-buying plan
sections.html:
Start with the well permit, construction report, pump information and the latest water-quality results. Then compare several nearby records in Highlands Ranch, Acres Green, Littleton, Louviers, Columbine Valley, Sterling Ranch and Lone Tree. Pay attention to wells targeting the same aquifer, not just the closest pin on a map.

For a vacant lot, have a Colorado-licensed driller review access, pad location, likely depth, casing and grout, power routing and the septic layout before closing. For an existing home, arrange a pump and flow test, inspect the pressure system, measure static and pumping levels and confirm the permit allows the intended use. Water rights can also affect a project: over-appropriated basins may require an augmentation plan, and a DWR permit controls what the well may legally supply.

Forty-five percent are under 100 feet, but 21% are 600 feet or deeper, so nearby records should guide the estimate.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Highlands Ranch?
faq.a: Permit records alone cannot establish that a well is safe to drink. Within about ten miles, mapped records include 205 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 25 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 18 historic mine features. Test the specific well, review its construction and repeat testing when site conditions or ownership change.
